readerTitle: What does it cost to say "only you"?
caseNote: 일반적인 관찰 (한 로스터리 원두만 쓰는 카페) + 가상 사례 (상업용 선반 제조사, 일정 관리 소프트웨어)
insight: 독점은 거래를 따내려고 덤으로 주는 호의가 아니라 내가 지불하는 가격이다. 따라서 대가를 확인하고 범위·지역·기간·조건을 좁혀서 판다.
misconception: 독점을 주면 파트너가 더 열심히 해 주니 무조건 이득이다. 또는 독점 요청은 무조건 거절해야 한다.

sources.text: 계약·유통 실무의 일반 개념 (독점 공급, 독점 유통, 최소 실적 조건)
카페와 로스터리의 독점 공급 관행은 업계의 일반적 관찰이며 특정 기업 사례가 아님
선반 제조사와 일정 관리 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 로스터리가 에스프레소 머신 대여, 교육, 가격 혜택을 주고 카페가 독점 구매를 약속하는 관행은 여러 시장에서 흔합니다. 다만 모든 카페가 그렇지는 않으므로 카드에는 "many", "may", "often"으로만 적었습니다. 게시 전에 업계 자료로 한 번 더 확인하세요.
지배적 사업자의 독점 거래가 많은 나라에서 경쟁 당국의 규제 대상이 될 수 있다는 내용은 일반론으로만 적었습니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언은 하지 않습니다.
레슨 안의 기간(5년, 3년, 12개월)과 조건은 모두 설명용 가상 수치이며 통계가 아닙니다.

cards.title: What does it cost to say "only you"?
body: Many cafés serve beans from just one roaster. Some even put up a small sign saying so.
It's often not only about taste. The roaster may have lent the espresso machine, trained the staff or offered a better price. In return, the café promised not to buy from anyone else.
That promise has a price. Most businesses forget to charge for it.

image.label: Café counter with a single coffee bag and a sign
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 카페 카운터에 에스프레소 머신과 원두 봉투 하나, 작은 팻말 "We only serve one roaster". 머신에 작은 꼬리표 "On loan". 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A distributor wants you all to itself.
body: You make commercial shelving in a small factory. A national distributor wants to carry your line.
Their condition: exclusive rights to every product you make, across the whole country, for five years. What do you answer?

options.text: Sign it. A national partner is a big win for a small factory
options.feedback: You get one strong channel fast. But you give up every other channel for five years, with nothing to fall back on if they underdeliver.

options.text: Say no. Never tie yourself to one partner
options.feedback: You keep all your options. But the distributor may not invest in selling your shelves at all, and you lose the deal.

options.text: Offer exclusivity in their strongest region for two years, kept only if they hit a minimum volume
options.feedback: They get protection for the work they put in. You keep the rest of the market and a way out if sales don't come.

cards.title: Exclusivity protects the partner's investment.
body: The distributor isn't just being greedy. To sell your shelving, it must train its sales reps, hold stock in its warehouses and pitch you to its customers.
If a rival distributor could sell the same shelves, it could ride on that work and undercut on price. So without some protection, the first distributor may never make the investment.
That's the real trade on the table: their effort for your options.

cards.title: Exclusivity
body: **Exclusivity** is a promise to deal with only one partner within a defined area, such as a product, a region or a type of customer.
It isn't a courtesy you add to close a deal. It's a price you pay. Every option you give up is a cost.
So the useful question isn't "exclusive, yes or no?" It's "what do I get for it, and how much of it am I selling?"

image.label: A scale: options given up versus partner commitment
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 접시에 "Options you give up" (다른 유통사, 다른 지역, 다른 채널 아이콘), 오른쪽 접시에 "What you get" (재고, 교육, 마케팅, 최소 물량 아이콘). 양쪽이 균형을 이루는 모습.

cards.title: Four dials on every exclusive deal.
body: You rarely have to choose between all or nothing. Each exclusive deal has dials you can turn.
list: **Territory or channel:** which region, which kind of customer
**Time:** how long, and whether it renews automatically
**Conditions:** what the partner must deliver to keep it, such as minimum volumes
cards.callout: All four set narrow can be a fair trade. All four set wide is a blank cheque.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the same dials apply to integration and marketplace deals: which features, which customer segment, how many months, and how many referrals the partner must send to keep the arrangement.

cards.title: Buyers sell exclusivity too.
body: It runs both ways. A buyer can promise to buy only from one supplier, like the café and its roaster. A seller can promise to sell only through one partner, like the shelving maker.
The logic is the same. One side gives up options. The other side invests or commits in return.
If you can't name what the other side is giving, you're handing out exclusivity for free.

cards.title: One partner means one point of failure.
body: Exclusivity concentrates risk. If your partner is acquired, loses focus or runs into trouble, your sales go with it. A minimum you can't enforce, with no way out, is just hope.
Size matters too. In many countries, exclusive deals by large or dominant companies can draw the attention of competition regulators. If you're the big player, get local legal advice before you sign.

cards.title: Now it's a software partnership.
body: You sell scheduling software to small clinics. A large payroll software company offers to build an integration and promote you to its customers.
Its condition: for three years, you don't integrate with any competing payroll tool. What do you do?

options.text: Accept. Their promotion could double your new users
options.feedback: You gain one big channel. But clinics using other payroll tools can't connect to you for three years, and those users may churn to a rival.

options.text: Accept a narrower version: they get featured partner status for 12 months, tied to a referral minimum, while your other integrations stay open
options.feedback: They still get something exclusive to justify their effort. You keep your product open and can walk away if referrals don't arrive.

options.text: Decline and integrate with everyone equally
options.feedback: You stay open to every customer. But the partner has little reason to promote you, so you may lose the channel that mattered most.

cards.title: Exclusivity is something you sell, so price it.
body: Before granting "only you," ask what the partner gives in return, then turn the dials: scope, territory, time and conditions.
**Try it today:** list every partner, supplier or channel deal you have. Mark any that limit who else you can work with. For each, write down what you got in exchange.
